title: Plan living and reception spaces
intro: Living-space planning starts with people and activities. Compare conversation and viewing arrangements, testing circulation and access against explicit acceptance points.
goals: Compare layouts using the same acceptance points

sections.title: Define activities and seating relationships
sections.text: Record everyday and guest occupancy and priorities for conversation, viewing or reading. Conversation needs reciprocal sightlines; viewing needs a suitable orientation to the screen from the intended seats. Seat count alone does not establish usability. Draw sightlines and identify seats requiring an awkward turn for the requested activity; do not derive seating comfort from screen size.
sections.caption: Judge sightlines against the intended activity.

sections.title: Test circulation during use
sections.text: Map routes from the entrance to destinations, including open doors, moved chairs and table use. Where the brief allows, keep through-traffic outside the conversation group. Measure the narrowest point in realistic operating states and compare it with documented user and project requirements. A clearance copied from an image is not a universal rule or evidence of accessibility compliance.
sections.caption: Measure bottlenecks in occupied and opening states.

sections.title: Compare layouts using the same acceptance points
sections.text: Keep room boundaries and assumed occupancy fixed when comparing A for conversation with B for viewing. Assess sightlines, through-routes, door opening and table access using the same criteria. Record trade-offs rather than changing drawing scale to flatter a proposal. Floor markings and a simple use mock-up can test positions before selection; symmetry alone is not a functional pass.
sections.caption: Use common criteria and state the trade-off.

example.title: Worked case and decision
example.text: The family prioritises conversation and daily balcony access. A faces seats toward each other but places a chair in the balcony route. B moves the chair to the side while retaining visual connection. Prefer B subject to checking the narrowest route and balcony door operation on site; an extra seat must not reintroduce the conflict.
example.decision: Decision: prefer B subject to route and door verification.

quiz.question: What makes the A/B comparison meaningful?
options: Shrink furniture in the favoured option
quiz.explanation: Fixed assumptions expose real functional differences.

assignment.prompt: Submit two same-scale layouts with activities, sightlines, circulation and acceptance criteria; justify the choice.

faq.question: Does symmetry prove a good layout?
faq.answer: No. Test activities, sightlines, routes and openings for the actual users.
